title: A local ring is a directed colimit of local rings essentially of finite type over Z

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00QU (lemma-limit-essentially-finite-type, line 32273), second and third paragraphs: $\Lambda$ the finite subsets $A\subset R$ ordered by inclusion, $R'_\lambda$ the sub-$\mathbf Z$-algebra generated by $A$, $R_\lambda$ its localization at $R'_\lambda\cap\mathfrak m$, and 'The assertion that $R=\colim R_\lambda$ is clear because all the maps $R_\lambda\to R$ are injective and any element of $R$ eventually is in the image'; the same system is the first half of the proof of Lemma Tag 00QT (lemma-limit-no-condition-local, line 32219). Used as 'we may first write $R=\colim R_\lambda$ as a directed colimit of local $\mathbf Z$-algebras which are essentially of finite type' in the proofs of Lemma Tag 00QX (line 32427) and Lemma Tag 00R7 (lemma-criterion-flatness-fibre, line 32992).

proof.text: Let $\Lambda$ be the finite subsets $A\subseteq R$, ordered by inclusion. It is nonempty since $\varnothing\in\Lambda$, and $A\cup B$ is a common upper bound of $A,B$. Put $C_A=\mathbf Z[A]\subseteq R$, the subring of polynomial expressions in the elements of $A$ with integer coefficients, and $q_A=C_A\cap\mathfrak m$. This is a prime ideal: $1\notin q_A$ and $ab\in q_A$ implies $a\in q_A$ or $b\in q_A$, since $\mathfrak m$ is maximal and hence prime. Define $R_A=(C_A)_{q_A}$ and $\mathfrak p_A=q_AR_A$ using [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. This definition gives that $R_A$ is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak p_A$. By [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], $C_A$ is of finite type over $\mathbf Z$, generated by the finite set $A$. Thus its localization $R_A$ is essentially of finite type over $\mathbf Z$ by [def-weil-pbc-essentially-finite-type-algebra].

source.place: Tag 00QU, lemma-limit-essentially-finite-type, second and third paragraphs of the proof (construction of the base system and its colimit)

proof.text: If $A\subseteq B$, then $C_A\subseteq C_B$ and $q_B\cap C_A=q_A$. For $s\in C_A\setminus q_A$, the same element lies outside $q_B$. Define $r_{BA}:R_A\to R_B$ by $a/s\mapsto a/s$. To check well-definedness, an equality in $R_A$ is witnessed by $u\in C_A\setminus q_A$ with $u(as'-a' s)=0$; the same equation and denominator $u$ witness equality in $R_B$. The usual fraction formulas for addition and multiplication show this is a ring map. It carries the generators $a/1$ of $q_AR_A$, $a\in q_A$, into $q_BR_B$, so is local. The formula gives $r_{AA}=\mathrm{id}$ and $r_{CB}r_{BA}=r_{CA}$ for $A\subseteq B\subseteq C$.

source.place: Tag 00QU, lemma-limit-essentially-finite-type, second and third paragraphs of the proof (construction of the base system and its colimit)

proof.text: For $s\in C_A\setminus q_A$ one has $s\notin\mathfrak m$, so [lem-weil-pbc-local-ring-unit-criterion] gives an inverse $s^{-1}\in R$. Define $\pi_A(a/s)=as^{-1}$. If $u(as'-a' s)=0$ witnesses equality of fractions, then $u,s,s'$ are units in $R$, so multiplication by their inverses gives $as^{-1}=a'(s')^{-1}$. The fraction formulas show that $\pi_A$ is a ring map, and $\pi_A(a/1)=a$ for $a\in C_A$. Since $\pi_A$ takes each generator of $q_AR_A$ into $\mathfrak m$, it is local. The same formula gives $\pi_Br_{BA}=\pi_A$. Moreover $\pi_A$ is injective: if $\pi_A(a/s)=\pi_A(b/t)$, multiplication by $st$ gives $at-bs=0$ in $R$, hence in the subring $C_A$; the equality criterion with witness $1$ gives $a/s=b/t$ in $R_A$.

source.place: Tag 00QU, lemma-limit-essentially-finite-type, second and third paragraphs of the proof (construction of the base system and its colimit)

proof.text: Every $x\in R$ is $\pi_{\{x\}}(x/1)$. We now check the universal property in [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. Let $T$ be any commutative ring and $f_A:R_A\to T$ ring maps with $f_Br_{BA}=f_A$ for $A\subseteq B$. Define $f(x)=f_A(y)$ whenever $\pi_A(y)=x$, a representation which exists by the preceding observation. If also $\pi_B(z)=x$, put $C=A\cup B$. Then $\pi_C(r_{CA}(y))=x=\pi_C(r_{CB}(z))$; injectivity of $\pi_C$ gives $r_{CA}(y)=r_{CB}(z)$, and compatibility gives $f_A(y)=f_B(z)$. Thus $f$ is well defined. For $x=\pi_A(y)$ and $x'=\pi_B(z)$, use their images in $R_{A\cup B}$: since both $\pi_{A\cup B}$ and $f_{A\cup B}$ are ring maps, this gives $f(x+x')=f(x)+f(x')$ and $f(xx')=f(x)f(x')$; representing $0,1$ at $\varnothing$ gives $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=1$. Hence $f$ is a ring map, and its defining formula gives $f\pi_A=f_A$ for all $A$. Any other such map takes $x=\pi_{\{x\}}(x/1)$ to $f_{\{x\}}(x/1)$, so equals $f$. This proves that the compatible local maps $\pi_A$ exhibit $R$ as the colimit in commutative rings.

lean.statement: theorem exists_local_essFiniteType_colimit (R : Type u) [CommRing R] [IsLocalRing R] : ∃ (I : Type u) (_ : Preorder I) (_ : Nonempty I) (_ : IsDirected I (· ≤ ·)) (F : I ⥤ CommRingCat.{u}) (π : F ⟶ (Functor.const I).obj (CommRingCat.of R)), (∀ i : I, IsLocalRing (F.obj i)) ∧ (∀ (i j : I) (f : i ⟶ j), IsLocalHom (F.map f).hom) ∧ (∀ i : I, IsLocalHom (π.app i).hom) ∧ Nonempty (IsColimit (Cocone.mk (CommRingCat.of R) π)) ∧ (∀ i : I, Algebra.EssFiniteType ℤ (F.obj i))
